title: Israel Salanter
hook: the story is told that he used little water for ritual washing, so the water-carrier wasn't overburdened

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: middot, measures. Your line was traits are measures: too little, too much, or the right amount. Where did a dial need turning? Today, a rabbi who measured even his water. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

Before eating bread, observant Jews wash their hands from a cup, pouring water over each hand and saying a blessing. It takes a few seconds. There's a story told about one rabbi at that cup. People watching him expected a famous teacher to pour generously, splash after splash, the way a devout person might. Instead he poured just a little, the least the law allowed, and set the cup down. Someone asked him why so little. His answer is the reason his name is today's word.
screen: `A CUP BEFORE THE BREAD.` → `HE POURED JUST A LITTLE.` → `SOMEONE ASKED WHY.`

segments.voice: Israel Salanter. Turn the story four ways. First, the answer. As the story is told, the water in that house was hauled up from a well by a worker, a water-carrier, bucket by bucket, on her back. Every extra splash at the cup was another trip to the well for someone else. So the rabbi said, in effect: I won't be pious at her expense. Second, why it surprised people. The Talmud praises generous washing. In tractate Shabbat, a rabbi says he washed with full handfuls of water and was given full handfuls of good. So pouring more was a real mitzvah, and here was a great teacher choosing less. He didn't skip the washing; he kept it, at the measure the law requires, and moved the extra devotion somewhere else: to the person carrying the buckets. Third, the man. Salanter was a rabbi in Lithuania whom tradition calls the father of the Mussar movement, the path of working on your traits one at a time. This story is Mussar in a single gesture. Yesterday's word said traits are measures. Here, even piety has a measure, and the scale includes other people's backs. Fourth, the other stories. People tell another one: before Passover, when he was asked what to watch for in a matzah bakery, he is said to have pointed to the women doing the kneading and said, in effect, don't overwork them. Whether every detail happened just this way, these stories are how his students remembered him. And they carry an ordinary question into an ordinary week. The long shower someone else cleans up after. The volunteer shift that leaves a coworker covering yours. Devotion is real, these stories say, and so is the person who pays for it.
screen: `THE WATER CAME FROM A WELL.` · `THE TALMUD PRAISES PLENTY OF WATER.` · `EVEN PIETY HAS A MEASURE.` · `WATCH THE ONES WHO KNEAD.` · then, large: `NOT PIOUS AT OTHERS' EXPENSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: consider someone else's labor. Settle, and breathe. Think of one good thing in your day that someone else made possible without being thanked. The person who cleans the office. The one who drives the bus, cooks the meal, answers the phone, empties the bins. Picture their hands at work. Then think of one thing you do, even a good thing, that adds to their load. Hold both pictures side by side. Nothing to fix right now; just see the buckets. If you pray, you can bring that person before God by name, in your own words. If you don't, simply hold them in your attention. The bell holds the time.
Israel Salanter. The rabbi tradition calls the father of the Mussar movement, remembered for pouring little water so the water-carrier would carry less. Today's word.
Your line: not pious at others' expense. Today, before one good deed, ask who carries the buckets for it, and lighten their load once. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Observant Jews wash their hands from a cup before eating bread, with a blessing; Mussar teachers often retell Rabbi Israel Salanter's washing story to teach that devotion should not burden other people.

pour the least the law requires.
fork.reveal: as the story is told, he poured just a little, kept the mitzvah, and spared the water-carrier the extra trips.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rabbi being careful with water.
what it means: a rabbi refusing to be pious at the expense of the worker who hauled it.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud praises abundant washing, so choosing the legal minimum was a pointed choice: the extra devotion moved to a person.

sources.ref: Stories told of Rabbi Israel Salanter

notes: The washing story circulates in several versions (a water-carrier, a maidservant; at home or as a guest). The lesson makes the carrier a woman and frames it as 'as the story is told'; confirm or neutralize the detail.
Shabbat 62b (Rav Chisda: one who washes with abundant water is given abundant good) is paraphrased; confirm the reference.
The matzah-bakery story is told as 'people tell another one'; confirm it is fair to attribute to Salanter.
'Tradition calls him the father of the Mussar movement' and 'a rabbi in Lithuania': no dates given on purpose. Y3 day 970 used the shoemaker's-candle story, so it is avoided here.
Original-language game set to null: no confident Hebrew spelling of his name worth teaching.
Editor pass: Shabbat 62b reworded as Rav Chisda's own report (full handfuls washed, full handfuls of good), not a general promise; cut the unsourced 'still retold in homes and study halls'.
